subcategory: improved culinary dandelion cultivar for salad greens

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil is workable, or in late summer for a fall/overwintered crop, in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in zone 3–9; Ameliore (a classic French heirloom, sometimes offered as 'Amélioré à Coeur Plein') is a cultivated culinary strain of common dandelion selected over generations for much larger, thicker, broader, and more tender leaves than wild dandelion, with a milder, less bitter flavor when grown quickly in rich soil.

directions: Direct sow Ameliore Dandelion seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; thin seedlings to 6–10 inches apart and keep evenly watered for fast, tender growth. Unlike lawn dandelion, this French culinary selection produces a dense rosette of broad, deeply notched, dark-green leaves that stay comparatively mild and non-bitter, especially when harvested young or blanched by covering the crown for 1–2 weeks before cutting. Leaves are cooked like a hearty green or used raw in salads for their distinctive earthy, slightly bitter edge that mellows with cooler weather; the taproot can also be dug, roasted, and ground as a caffeine-free coffee substitute. A cut-and-come-again crop, it regrows readily after repeated harvest and tolerates light frost, making it useful for extending the salad-green season into early spring and late fall.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in zone 8–11, or grow in a large container and overwinter indoors in colder zones; Golden Bay is a slow-growing sport of common bay laurel selected for young foliage that emerges bright chartreuse-gold, aging to deep green, giving an ornamental two-tone shrub that is fully usable in the kitchen exactly like standard bay leaf.

directions: Plant Golden Bay in well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest gold color, or partial shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch; water moderately and protect from harsh winter wind, which can damage foliage below the high 10s °F. Give it more shelter and shade than plain green bay, since the golden foliage is more prone to sunburn in intense heat. Prune to shape and to harvest leaves — the aromatic, leathery gold-and-green leaves are dried and used exactly like ordinary bay laurel in soups, stews, braises, and stocks, with identical flavor to the green form. Grown as much for its bright, formal, topiary-friendly foliage as for cooking, it is a popular container specimen for patios and entryways in cooler climates where it can be moved indoors over winter.

subcategory: pink-flowered culinary and medicinal hyssop cultivar

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost, surface-sown or barely covered, in full sun in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in zone 3–9; Pink Hyssop is a true-breeding rose-pink-flowered seed strain of common hyssop, otherwise identical in aromatic foliage and culinary/medicinal use to the standard blue-flowered species, grown both for kitchen and tea use and as a color variant for pollinator borders.

directions: Sow Pink Hyssop indoors in a warm, well-drained starting mix; transplant after hardening off into lean, dry to moderately moist, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun. Prune back hard after the first flush of bloom to maintain a dense, bushy shape and to encourage rebloom later in the season. The rose-pink flower spikes are showier in the border than the species type and equally attractive to bees and butterflies, while the strongly camphor-scented leaves are harvested the same way as standard hyssop for use in bittering liqueurs, savory meat rubs, and traditional expectorant teas. Being a seed strain rather than a clone, plants show some minor variation in exact flower shade from pale to deep rose; select and propagate the best-colored individuals by cuttings if uniform color is desired.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in zone 9–11, or grow in containers and overwinter indoors elsewhere; Chocolate Mint Geranium is a hybrid scented pelargonium (oak-leaf type parentage) with large, velvety, deeply lobed light-green leaves marked with a broad chocolate-brown central blotch and a mild, minty aroma distinct from the smaller, plain-green leaves of the true Peppermint Geranium.

directions: Root Chocolate Mint Geranium cuttings in well-drained, lean soil; grow in full sun to partial shade and let the soil dry between waterings, as it is prone to root rot when kept wet. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep the somewhat sprawling habit compact and bushy. The bold, velvety leaves — bright green edged in a broad chocolate-brown central patch — carry a soft, mild mint fragrance when brushed or crushed, making the plant a striking foliage accent in containers as much as a kitchen herb. Use the leaves sparingly to flavor cream, sugar, and iced tea, or simply grow it for its ornamental two-tone foliage among a scented-geranium collection; bring indoors as a houseplant before first fall frost since it has no cold tolerance.
sources: Herb Society of America — scented geraniums complete guide

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Lady Plymouth is a classic variegated sport of Rose Geranium with finely cut, grey-green leaves edged in an irregular creamy-white margin, carrying the same strong rose fragrance and culinary use as plain Rose Geranium but valued additionally as a specimen foliage plant for its ornamental variegation.

directions: Root Lady Plymouth cuttings in lean, well-drained soil and grow in full sun to partial shade with light, infrequent watering, allowing soil to dry between waterings; overly rich soil or heavy shade will dull both the variegation and the fragrance. Pinch stems regularly to maintain a full, shrubby shape and remove any all-green reverted shoots as soon as they appear to keep the variegated pattern true. The finely dissected, rose-and-lemon-scented leaves are used exactly like standard Rose Geranium — infused in sugar, cream, and jellies, or added fresh to fruit salads and iced drinks — while the cream-edged foliage additionally makes this one of the most ornamental scented geraniums for mixed containers and hanging baskets. Bring indoors well before first frost as a houseplant, since it has no cold hardiness.
